payload.court: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Court Of Small Causes Bengaluru
payload.holding: The tribunal held that the insurer proved a fundamental breach of policy conditions due to the driver lacking a valid driving licence, but directed the insurer to pay the compensation to the petitioner in the first instance under the 'pay and recover' principle, with liberty to recover the same from the vehicle owner.
payload.ratio: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, absolving the insurer of direct liability; however, to protect third-party rights, the insurer may be ordered to pay the compensation first and subsequently recover it from the owner.

More often than not, literal interpretation of a statute or a provision of a statute results in absurdity.
Therefore, while interpreting statutory provisions, the Courts should keep in mind the objectives or
purpose for which statute has been enacted. Justice Frankfurter of U.S. Supreme Court in an article
titled as Some Reflections on the Reading of Statutes (47 Columbia Law Reports 527), observed that,
"legislation has an aim, it seeks to obviate some mischief, to supply an adequacy, to effect a change
of policy, to formulate a plan of Government. That aim, that policy is not drawn, like nitrogen, out of
the air; it is evidenced in the language of the statutes, as read in the light of other external
manifestations of purpose".

args.question: What must an owner do to check a driver's licence before employing them, and does failing to check defeat the insurer's defence?

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: The owner has a responsibility to take adequate care to see that the driver has an appropriate licence. When hiring a driver, the owner must check whether the driver has a valid driving licence. If the driver produces a licence that looks genuine on its face, the owner is not expected to verify with the RTO whether it was actually issued by a competent authority.
supporting.fact_alignment: The owner remained ex parte and adduced no evidence of having checked the driver's licence. The court held that since the driver produced a licence with a 'transport vehicle' endorsement, the owner was prima facie satisfied, and the insurer failed to prove conscious breach.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most directly on-point judgment in the corpus. It quotes Lehru (2003) 3 SCC 338 verbatim on the owner's duty: the owner must check the licence, but if it looks genuine, no further enquiry is expected. The insurer must prove the owner knew or noticed the licence was fake.
supporting.quote: When an owner is hiring a driver he will therefore have to check whether the driver has a driving licence. If the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, the owner is not expected to find out whether the licence has in fact been issued by a competent authority or not. ... Thus where the owner has satisfied himself that the driver has a licence and is driving competently there would be no breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii).

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The breach of policy conditions must be conscious and wilful on the part of the insured. Even if a conscious breach is established, the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver possessed only an LMV (non-transport) licence but was driving a goods vehicle. The insurer proved the breach but was still directed to pay and recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that the insurer's defence (breach of licence condition) does not defeat the claim against the insurer — it only entitles the insurer to recover from the owner. The third party is always protected.
supporting.quote: It is well settled that the breach must be conscious and wilful. Even if a conscious breach on the part of the insured is established, still the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence is a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy. However, the insurer must pay the third-party claimant first and then recover from the owner under the 'pay and recover' principle.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no licence at all. The owner failed to produce the driver's licence despite being represented by counsel. The insurer proved the breach.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even in the strongest case for the insurer (driver had zero licence, owner failed to produce any evidence), the remedy is pay-and-recover, not avoidance of liability to the third party.
supporting.quote: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, absolving the insurer of direct liability; however, to protect third-party rights, the insurer may be ordered to pay the compensation first and subsequently recover it from the owner.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where a driver holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation/badge required for a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV licence but no badge/authorisation to drive a tourist maxi cab (transport vehicle). The insurer proved the breach through the Motor Vehicles Inspector's evidence.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even where the insurer successfully proves the licence defect, the remedy is pay-and-recover, not outright rejection of the claim.
supporting.quote: The doctrine of 'pay and recover' has been recognised by the Supreme Court in several decisions.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
supporting.principle: When a driving licence is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum period. The insurer must pay the third party and recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence expired on 30-04-2008, the accident was on 02-07-2008, and the licence was renewed on 04-07-2008. The insurer proved the breach.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that even an expired-but-subsequently-renewed licence scenario results in pay-and-recover, not avoidance.
supporting.quote: Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded either from the owner or the driver, as the vehicle in question is insured, the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: For driving a goods carriage carrying dangerous/hazardous goods, a special endorsement on the driving licence is mandatory. The absence thereof constitutes a breach entitling the insurer to pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had a valid licence for MC, LMV, HGV, HTV but no special endorsement for hazardous goods. The tanker was carrying such goods.
supporting.why_it_matters: Extends the owner's duty to verify not just the existence of a licence but also the specific endorsements required for the type of vehicle/goods. Rule 132(5) of CMVR casts a duty on the owner to ensure the driver holds the correct licence.
supporting.quote: As per Rule 132 (5) of Central Motor Vehicles Rule, 1989, it is the duty of the owner to ensure that the driver of the goods carriage carrying dangerous or hazardous goods holds a driving license as per the rule 9 of the aforesaid Central Motor Vehicles Rules.

adverse.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
adverse.principle: The owner has a duty to check the driver's licence. If the owner fails to adduce evidence of having done so, the insurer may be entitled to pay-and-recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that the owner's duty is limited to a facial check — if the licence looks genuine, the owner is not expected to verify with the RTO. This narrows the scope of the owner's obligation and makes it harder for the insurer to prove 'conscious breach'.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The judgment itself supports the insurer's right to pay-and-recover where the owner fails to produce evidence of having checked. The risk is that it limits what the owner must do — but it does not eliminate the owner's duty entirely. The insurer can argue that on the facts, the owner did not even perform the basic facial check (e.g., the licence was for a completely different class of vehicle, or no licence was produced at all).
adverse.quote: When an owner is hiring a driver he will therefore have to check whether the driver has a driving licence. If the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, the owner is not expected to find out whether the licence has in fact been issued by a competent authority or not.

adverse.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
adverse.principle: An insurer cannot avoid liability to third parties merely because the driver of an LMV did not have a specific endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that the licence defect was not 'fundamental' and therefore the insurer cannot even get a pay-and-recover order. This is a Supreme Court judgment and directly limits the insurer's defence.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case turned on the specific finding that a Mahindra Maxi Cab is a light motor vehicle and the driver held a valid LMV licence. The Supreme Court held that the absence of a 'commercial vehicle' endorsement on an LMV licence is not a fundamental breach. The insurer can distinguish this where: (a) the driver had no licence at all; (b) the driver had a licence for a completely different class (e.g., two-wheeler driving a heavy vehicle); or (c) the vehicle was not an LMV but a transport vehicle requiring a specific badge/endorsement under state rules.
adverse.quote: Merely because the driver did not get any endorsement in the driving licence to drive Mahindra Maxi Cab, which is a light motor vehicle, the High Court has committed grave error of law in holding that the insurer is not liable to pay compensation because the driver was not holding the licence to drive the commercial vehicle.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: The mere non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence on the date of accident does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer of third-party liability.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that an expired licence (especially one renewed shortly after) is not a fundamental breach, and the insurer remains liable without even a pay-and-recover order.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This is a 2001 Tribunal decision that predates the Supreme Court's clarification in Ram Babu Tiwari (which doc_003 follows). The later position is that if renewal is sought more than 30 days after expiry, the licence is valid only from the renewal date, and the interregnum period is uncovered. The insurer can argue that the later Supreme Court position prevails.
adverse.quote: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party under the Motor Vehicles Act regardless of any policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: Swaran Singh's principles apply only to third-party claims, not own-damage claims. A fake licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimant will cite this to argue that in third-party claims (which this is), the insurer must pay and recover — which is actually consistent with the insurer's position. However, the claimant may also argue that the insurer's burden to prove the licence was fake is heavy and requires positive evidence.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This judgment actually supports the insurer's position on the pay-and-recover remedy for third-party claims. The risk is low because it confirms rather than undermines the insurer's right to recovery. The only risk is the high evidentiary burden it places on the insurer to prove the licence was fake.
adverse.quote: In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.

priority_arguments: 1. The insurer's statutory liability to third parties under Section 149 MV Act is not defeated by a licence breach — the remedy is always pay-and-recover (doc_024, doc_033, doc_035).

2. The owner's duty is limited: they must check the licence, but if it looks genuine on its face, they are not expected to verify with the RTO (doc_027, quoting Lehru). The insurer must prove the owner knew or noticed the licence was fake.
3. The burden of proving conscious and wilful breach is on the insurer — mere absence of a licence or an invalid licence does not automatically establish breach by the owner (doc_033, doc_027).
4. Where the driver had no licence at all, or a licence for a completely different class of vehicle, the breach is fundamental and pay-and-recover is clearly available (doc_024).
5. For special categories (hazardous goods, transport vehicles requiring badges), specific endorsements are mandatory and the owner has an additional duty to verify these (doc_001, doc_035).
6. If the owner remained ex parte or failed to produce the driver's licence, an adverse inference can be drawn that the owner did not check the licence (doc_024, doc_027).
strategy.compensation_range: Not applicable — this is a liability/defence question, not a quantum question.
risks: 1. S.Iyyapan (doc_032) — Supreme Court holds that absence of a commercial endorsement on an LMV licence is not a fundamental breach. This could defeat the insurer's defence entirely if the vehicle is an LMV and the driver held an LMV licence, even without the transport endorsement.

2. The Lehru principle (cited in doc_027) limits the owner's duty to a facial check — if the licence looks genuine, the owner is not expected to verify with the RTO. This makes it harder to prove conscious breach.
3. K.G. Srinivasamurthy (doc_034) suggests that an expired-but-renewed licence is not a fundamental breach — though this is weakened by later Supreme Court authority (Ram Babu Tiwari).

4. The insurer bears the entire burden of proof to establish both the licence defect AND the owner's conscious breach — if the owner adduces evidence of having checked the licence, the defence may fail.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: In the claim petition, the insurer should: (a) lead positive evidence of the licence defect (RTO verification report, examining the Motor Vehicles Inspector); (b) examine the owner/driver to establish that the owner did not check the licence or knew it was invalid; (c) seek a specific finding of conscious/wilful breach; and (d) in any event, seek a pay-and-recover order. The insurer should NOT argue for complete exoneration from third-party liability — the consistent line of authority holds that the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the owner.

caveats: This corpus does not contain the full text of Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297 or Lehru (2003) 3 SCC 338, which are the foundational Supreme Court authorities on this issue. They are cited extensively in the corpus judgments and their principles are applied, but the original judgments are not in the corpus.

The corpus contains no judgment from the Supreme Court directly on what constitutes 'adequate' verification by the owner beyond the Lehru principle (facial check). The question of whether an owner must, for example, check the licence online or call the RTO is not addressed in any corpus judgment.

Doc_031 (Laxmi Narain Dhut) is a Supreme Court judgment that limits Swaran Singh to third-party claims — this is relevant context but the present question concerns third-party claims where Swaran Singh does apply.

payload.court: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal Ratlam / Madhya Pradesh High Court
payload.holding: The High Court held that the insurer is not liable to pay compensation for the death of a gratuitous passenger carried in a goods vehicle, dismissed the owners' appeal regarding negligence and quantum, and dismissed the claimants' cross-objections for enhancement.
payload.ratio: Where a passenger travelling in a goods vehicle is a gratuitous passenger whose risk is not statutorily required to be covered under Section 95 of the Motor Vehicles Act and is not covered by the terms of the insurance policy, the insurer cannot be held liable for compensation.

priority_arguments: 1. The insurer's statutory liability to third parties under Section 149 MV Act is not defeated by a licence breach — the remedy is always pay-and-recover (doc_024, doc_033, doc_035, doc_025).

2. The owner's duty is limited: they must check the licence, but if it looks genuine on its face, they are not expected to verify with the RTO (doc_027, quoting Lehru). The insurer must prove the owner knew or noticed the licence was fake.

3. The burden of proving conscious and wilful breach is on the insurer — mere absence of a licence or an invalid licence does not automatically establish breach by the owner (doc_033, doc_027, doc_025).
4. Where the driver had no licence at all, or a licence for a completely different class of vehicle, the breach is fundamental and pay-and-recover is clearly available (doc_024).
5. For special categories (hazardous goods, transport vehicles requiring badges), specific endorsements are mandatory and the owner has an additional duty to verify these (doc_001, doc_035).
6. If the owner remained ex parte or failed to produce the driver's licence, an adverse inference can be drawn that the owner did not check the licence (doc_024, doc_027).
strategy.compensation_range: Not applicable — this is a liability/defence question, not a quantum question.
risks: 1. S.Iyyapan (doc_032) — Supreme Court holds that absence of a commercial endorsement on an LMV licence is not a fundamental breach. This could defeat the insurer's defence entirely if the vehicle is an LMV and the driver held an LMV licence, even without the transport endorsement. HIGH risk.

2. The Lehru principle (cited in doc_027) limits the owner's duty to a facial check — if the licence looks genuine, the owner is not expected to verify with the RTO. This makes it harder to prove conscious breach. MEDIUM risk.
3. K.G. Srinivasamurthy (doc_034) suggests that an expired-but-renewed licence is not a fundamental breach — though this is weakened by later Supreme Court authority (Ram Babu Tiwari). MEDIUM risk.
4. Yallavva (doc_025) imposes a double burden on the insurer: prove the owner failed to exercise reasonable care AND prove the breach was fundamental/contributed to the accident. MEDIUM risk.

5. The insurer bears the entire burden of proof to establish both the licence defect AND the owner's conscious breach — if the owner adduces evidence of having checked the licence, the defence may fail.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: In the claim petition, the insurer should: (a) lead positive evidence of the licence defect (RTO verification report, examining the Motor Vehicles Inspector); (b) examine the owner/driver to establish that the owner did not check the licence or knew it was invalid; (c) seek a specific finding of conscious/wilful breach; and (d) in any event, seek a pay-and-recover order. The insurer should NOT argue for complete exoneration from third-party liability — the consistent line of authority holds that the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the owner.

caveats: doc_006 (National Insurance Co. vs Meena) — This judgment primarily concerns contributory negligence and quantum. It contains a pay-and-recover order for a licence breach but adds nothing beyond what doc_024, doc_033, and doc_035 already establish. It also cites S.Iyyapan (doc_032) which is already in the adverse list. Not separately adverse or supporting beyond the existing authorities.

doc_014 (Shivlal vs Rukmabai) — This is about gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles under the 1939 Act. The issue is whether the insurer is liable for passengers not covered by the policy. It has nothing to do with driver's licence verification or the owner's duty to check a licence. Completely unrelated.

doc_016 (Reserved On vs State of HP) — This is a criminal revision concerning rash and negligent driving. The only licence point is that absence of a licence does not constitute rashness/negligence in criminal law. It does not address the owner's duty to verify a driver's licence or the insurer's defence in civil compensation proceedings. Not relevant.

doc_028 (United India Insurance vs Sukumarbai) — This concerns passengers travelling in a private vehicle for hire or reward, where the insurer was exonerated because the passenger was not a 'third party' under the Act policy. The issue is the scope of third-party coverage for passengers, not driver's licence verification. Not relevant.

This corpus does not contain the full text of Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297 or Lehru (2003) 3 SCC 338, which are the foundational Supreme Court authorities on this issue. They are cited extensively in the corpus judgments and their principles are applied, but the original judgments are not in the corpus.

The corpus contains no judgment from the Supreme Court directly on what constitutes 'adequate' verification by the owner beyond the Lehru principle (facial check). The question of whether an owner must, for example, check the licence online or call the RTO is not addressed in any corpus judgment.

priority_arguments: 1. The insurer's statutory liability to third parties under Section 149 MV Act is not defeated by a licence breach — the remedy is always pay-and-recover (doc_024, doc_033, doc_035, doc_025).

2. The owner's duty is limited: they must check the licence, but if it looks genuine on its face, they are not expected to verify with the RTO (doc_027, quoting Lehru). The insurer must prove the owner knew or noticed the licence was fake.

3. The burden of proving conscious and wilful breach is on the insurer — mere absence of a licence or an invalid licence does not automatically establish breach by the owner (doc_033, doc_027, doc_025).
4. Where the driver had no licence at all, or a licence for a completely different class of vehicle, the breach is fundamental and pay-and-recover is clearly available (doc_024).
5. For special categories (hazardous goods, transport vehicles requiring badges), specific endorsements are mandatory and the owner has an additional duty to verify these (doc_001, doc_035).
6. If the owner remained ex parte or failed to produce the driver's licence, an adverse inference can be drawn that the owner did not check the licence (doc_024, doc_027).
strategy.compensation_range: Not applicable — this is a liability/defence question, not a quantum question.
risks: 1. S.Iyyapan (doc_032) — Supreme Court holds that absence of a commercial endorsement on an LMV licence is not a fundamental breach. This could defeat the insurer's defence entirely if the vehicle is an LMV and the driver held an LMV licence, even without the transport endorsement. HIGH risk.

2. The Lehru principle (cited in doc_027) limits the owner's duty to a facial check — if the licence looks genuine, the owner is not expected to verify with the RTO. This makes it harder to prove conscious breach. MEDIUM risk.
3. K.G. Srinivasamurthy (doc_034) suggests that an expired-but-renewed licence is not a fundamental breach — though this is weakened by later Supreme Court authority (Ram Babu Tiwari). MEDIUM risk.
4. Yallavva (doc_025) imposes a double burden on the insurer: prove the owner failed to exercise reasonable care AND prove the breach was fundamental/contributed to the accident. MEDIUM risk.

5. The insurer bears the entire burden of proof to establish both the licence defect AND the owner's conscious breach — if the owner adduces evidence of having checked the licence, the defence may fail.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: In the claim petition, the insurer should: (a) lead positive evidence of the licence defect (RTO verification report, examining the Motor Vehicles Inspector); (b) examine the owner/driver to establish that the owner did not check the licence or knew it was invalid; (c) seek a specific finding of conscious/wilful breach; and (d) in any event, seek a pay-and-recover order. The insurer should NOT argue for complete exoneration from third-party liability — the consistent line of authority holds that the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the owner.

caveats: doc_006 (National Insurance Co. vs Meena) — This judgment primarily concerns contributory negligence and quantum. It contains a pay-and-recover order for a licence breach but adds nothing beyond what doc_024, doc_033, and doc_035 already establish. It also cites S.Iyyapan (doc_032) which is already in the adverse list. Not separately adverse or supporting beyond the existing authorities.

doc_014 (Shivlal vs Rukmabai) — This is about gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles under the 1939 Act. The issue is whether the insurer is liable for passengers not covered by the policy. It has nothing to do with driver's licence verification or the owner's duty to check a licence. Completely unrelated.

doc_016 (Reserved On vs State of HP) — This is a criminal revision concerning rash and negligent driving. The only licence point is that absence of a licence does not constitute rashness/negligence in criminal law. It does not address the owner's duty to verify a driver's licence or the insurer's defence in civil compensation proceedings. Not relevant.

doc_028 (United India Insurance vs Sukumarbai) — This concerns passengers travelling in a private vehicle for hire or reward, where the insurer was exonerated because the passenger was not a 'third party' under the Act policy. The issue is the scope of third-party coverage for passengers, not driver's licence verification. Not relevant.

They are cited extensively in the corpus judgments and their principles are applied, but the original judgments are not in the corpus.

The corpus contains no judgment from the Supreme Court directly on what constitutes 'adequate' verification by the owner beyond the Lehru principle (facial check). The question of whether an owner must, for example, check the licence online or call the RTO is not addressed in any corpus judgment.
